# Writing clearly

Clear writing is not short writing. It is writing whose shape matches the shape
of the idea, so a reader spends their attention on the idea rather than on the
sentence. This skill covers the three edits that recover the most clarity per
minute spent, and the one edit that is almost always a mistake.

## Start from the claim

A paragraph that opens with context and closes with the claim forces the reader
to hold the context in working memory until the claim arrives. Reverse it. Put
the claim in the first sentence and spend the rest of the paragraph supporting
it. The reader can then decide, cheaply, whether to keep reading.

### When the claim is genuinely conditional

Some claims only hold under a condition, and stating the claim first would be
wrong rather than merely unconventional. In that case state the condition in a
subordinate clause and keep the claim in the main clause, so the grammar still
puts the claim in the position of emphasis.

## Cut the throat-clearing

The first two sentences of a draft are usually the writer warming up. Delete
them and read what is left. If it still starts, they were throat-clearing.

Common forms of throat-clearing:

- Restating the title as a sentence.
- Announcing the structure of a piece that is under a thousand words.
- Apologising for the length before writing anything.

## Prefer the concrete noun

Abstractions are cheap to write and expensive to read. Every abstract noun is a
small tax on the reader, who must instantiate it before the sentence resolves.

> The difference between the almost right word and the right word is really a
> large matter — 'tis the difference between the lightning bug and the
> lightning.

## The edit that is usually a mistake

Deleting every adverb. The rule exists because weak adverbs prop up weak verbs,
not because adverbs are bad. An adverb that changes the meaning of a sentence is
doing real work, and removing it removes the meaning.

## Checking your own draft

Read the draft aloud. Anywhere you run out of breath, the sentence is long
enough to be worth splitting. Anywhere you stumble, the reader will stumble too.
